cards.explanation: The answer is holiness. The writer says, “Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.” Peace and holiness come as a pair here, like dough and an oven. That's verse 14, friends.

The answer is that it would cause trouble and defile many. The writer says a root of bitterness would “…cause trouble and defile many.” Notice the word many. One root, and it doesn't stay in one spot. I think that's why he tells them to watch out for each other.

The answer is a single meal. The writer says Esau “…for a single meal sold his birthright.” Genesis 25:34 says Jacob gave him bread and lentil stew. That's one meal, friends. A birthright is a LOT to trade for a bowl of stew.

The answer is True. The writer says Esau “…could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.” The tears are right there in verse 17. I think that makes this a heavy part to read, and I don't want to rush past it.
The answer is darkness, gloom and storm. The writer lists “…darkness, gloom, and storm…” right alongside the fire. Fire, dark and a storm all at once. Even I'd stay home with the oven mitts on.

The word is stoned. The writer says the people could not bear what was commanded: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned.” It comes from Exodus 19:12-13. Even an animal. That tells you how serious the boundary was.

The answer is False. Moses did not stay calm. The writer says the sight was so terrifying that even Moses, Israel's leader, said, “I am trembling with fear.” Even Moses. That word even says a lot, friends.

The answer is Mount Zion. The writer says, “Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.” After all that fire and storm, that word Instead feels like a deep breath. And I'll take a deep breath any day.

The word is heaven. The writer says you have come to “…the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven.” Enrolled, like a name written down on a list. I think there's something comforting about being on that list, friends.

The answer is the mediator of a new covenant. The writer says you have come “…to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant…” A mediator stands between two sides. A new covenant also means something new is happening. That's good news after that scary mountain.

The answer is True. The writer says you have come to “…the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.” Abel was killed by his brother Cain (Genesis 4:8), and God told Cain, “Your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). So both bloods speak, and the writer says one speaks better.

The answer is that we will escape even less. The writer says, “…how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven?” The people did not escape when they refused Him on earth, and the writer says it's even less for us if we reject Him from heaven. That's a serious line, and it's worth sitting with.
The answer is False. The promise says, “Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well.” So the earth is shaken, and heaven as well. The word only would break the verse.

The word is unshakable. The writer says “Once more” signifies the removal of what can be shaken, “…so that the unshakable may remain.” The shaken things are created things. What's left is the unshakable. I'd say that's a good thing to be holding onto.

The answer is acceptably with reverence and awe. The writer says, “…let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe.” Notice the order, friends. Gratitude comes first, and the worship follows from it. I like that.
